_readme: Plain-language summaries shown under each paper. The key can be any identifier ADS lists for the paper: its arXiv id (e.g. 2606.03375), its bibcode, or its DOI. Papers without an entry here simply show the ADS abstract instead. Edit freely; this file is never overwritten by the ADS update.
2606.03375: JWST keeps finding surprisingly compact, red objects in the early Universe, the 'Little Red Dots', and astronomers disagree on whether they are dense swarms of stars or black holes growing inside dust. High-resolution cosmological simulations of environments with very efficient star formation naturally build such compact galaxies: up to a few hundred million solar masses of stars packed into a few hundred parsecs. In them, gas inflows, gravitational torques and stellar friction can funnel enough material to the centre to make a ~10^6 solar-mass black hole. So the 'stars' and 'AGN' pictures may be two stages of the same story rather than rivals.
2602.21002: Many Little Red Dots show no X-ray emission, which is odd if each hosts a growing black hole. This paper tests whether black holes born from runaway stellar collisions inside these systems can be reconciled with the X-ray upper limits, by modelling both seed formation and the X-rays it would produce. The answer is yes, if the galaxies are compact enough (a steep size-mass relation), and the X-ray weakness can come from heavy obscuration or moderately sub-Eddington growth. Even if LRDs start as starbursts, they should eventually turn into AGN.
2412.08280: Galaxies around 10^10 solar masses often host both a nuclear star cluster and a supermassive black hole, hinting that the two share an origin. Here the Galacticus galaxy-formation model is extended so that nuclear star clusters grow 'in situ' from gas funnelled to a galaxy's centre, and so that stellar collisions inside them can seed black holes. More compact clusters are better seed factories, producing light, medium and heavy seeds that grow to ~10^9 solar masses and match the observed black-hole mass function above 10^8 solar masses. The cluster population also agrees with observations in shape, though quantitative agreement still needs refinement.
2603.24550: JWST, helped by gravitational lensing, has revealed young massive star clusters in the early Universe. This work shows that roughly 16% of them are dense enough to undergo core collapse and runaway collisions, a recipe for intermediate-mass black holes. Above ~6 million solar masses, such clusters can also hold on to their gas despite supernova feedback, which could speed up the growth of the central object even further.
2605.20381: Estimates how massive a black hole can form by runaway collisions in the dense JWST-detected clusters, such as the 'Cosmic Gems' arc and the 'Firefly Sparkle'. Using a Fokker-Planck model plus an analytic treatment of collisions and stellar winds (validated against N-body simulations), it finds typical black-hole masses of ~100 to 4,000 solar masses, a formation efficiency of a few percent. The extremely compact Cosmic Gems clusters can reach 1,600-2,700 solar masses, but only at very low metallicity, otherwise stellar winds strip the seed's mass.
2305.18629: Supermassive black holes already exist less than a billion years after the Big Bang, and how they got so big so fast is still open. This early study uses the Galacticus semi-analytic galaxy-formation model to predict the black-hole population under different seeding scenarios. Black holes grow mainly through galaxy mergers and gas accretion, and by estimating each black hole's radius of influence the paper identifies which part of the population could be detected by future telescopes such as the ELT.
2024BAAA...65..205L: Conference proceedings summarising the first results of the model in which black-hole seeds form through stellar collisions inside nuclear star clusters, implemented in the Galacticus galaxy-formation code. This work was developed further in the 2025 Astronomy & Astrophysics paper.
2509.20453: Asks what happens to Little Red Dots if they are purely dense stellar systems. Their ages are comparable to their collision times and shorter than their relaxation times, a regime never observed before and prone to runaway collisions. In a fair fraction of them, a massive black hole is hard to avoid. That would explain why they look transient, why most are X-ray quiet (the black hole has not formed yet), and why they may be the best places to catch a newborn heavy black-hole seed.
2405.12008: Looks at how efficiently star clusters can turn their stars into a black hole through collisions. By comparing simulations and observations of nuclear star clusters, globular clusters and ultra-compact dwarf galaxies, the paper defines a critical cluster mass set by collision time, age and structure. Systems whose initial mass exceeds that critical mass reach black-hole formation efficiencies of 30-100%.
2611.07546: Massive stellar systems at high redshift may evolve far faster than their formal two-body relaxation time suggests, especially if they are built from many smaller clusters. The paper shows how a cluster's early 'cold collapse' separates its most massive stars from the rest, and gives a criterion for when they decouple. The most promising route to a central massive black hole is the cold collapse of a dense, massive cluster after few mergers or none, while repeated mergers instead produce larger, more extended systems.
